content.overview: Article 226 is the High Court gateway for Public Interest Litigation. It may be used to enforce fundamental rights and also other legal rights for any other purpose, subject to territorial limits and judicial restraint on standing. Liberalised standing still requires bona fide public interest; private disputes dressed as PIL fail.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Is a fundamental right or other legal right engaged? (2) Is the High Court territorially competent? (3) Is the petitioner acting bona fide in public interest? (4) Is Article 226 preferable to Article 32 on the facts? (5) Is the claim a private dispute in disguise?
content.study:
Core rule: Article 226 empowers every High Court to issue directions, orders or writs for enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose. PIL uses that power with liberalised standing so that public wrongs and rights of disadvantaged classes can be litigated in the High Courts.

What Article 226 supplies: High Court jurisdiction that is wider than Article 32 in the kinds of rights enforceable — fundamental rights and other legal rights — subject to the territorial reach of the High Court and established limits on writ process.

What liberal standing adds: A bona fide public-interest petitioner may be heard for others who cannot approach, or to compel public duties, without turning every policy disagreement into a maintainable petition.

Territorial and practical fit: Article 226 is often the first and natural forum for region-specific public wrongs, local statutory duties, and matters where the cause of action arises within the High Court's territory. Article 32 remains the Supreme Court Part III gateway when fundamental-rights enforcement at that level is appropriate.

Abuse filters: Private, contractual, and service disputes labelled as PIL fail. Busybodies and motivated petitions may be refused with costs. See limits-and-costs.

Current-law framing: Ground the analysis in Article 226, territorial competence, and bona fide public interest. Cross-read the constitutional Article 226 topic for writ-power and territorial detail. Case-law verification remains a separate gate; no holding is treated as verified solely from study text.

sections.heading: Article 226 as the High Court PIL gateway
sections.body: Article 226 is the principal High Court writ provision. For PIL, it is the door through which public-interest claims enter the High Court — whether to enforce fundamental rights or other legal rights for any other purpose — subject to territory and maintainability.

sections.heading: Wider rights base than Article 32
sections.body: Unlike Article 32, which is confined to fundamental rights in the Supreme Court, Article 226 reaches fundamental rights and other legal rights. That wider base makes High Court PIL suitable for many statutory and public-duty claims that are not framed purely as Part III violations.

sections.heading: Territorial limits
sections.body: High Court writ power is territorially bounded. The petition must connect to the High Court's territory through the seat of the authority, the cause of action, or other accepted territorial links. Liberal standing does not erase territorial competence.

sections.heading: Liberalised standing and bona fides
sections.body: A bona fide public-interest petitioner may move the High Court for rights of persons who cannot approach or to enforce public duties. Good faith and public character remain essential. Private rivalries and publicity petitions fail the test.

sections.heading: Forum choice: Article 226 or Article 32
sections.body: Prefer Article 226 for region-specific wrongs, non-Part-III public duties, and matters where the High Court is the suitable first forum. Prefer Article 32 when the claim is Supreme Court enforcement of fundamental rights. Forum choice is reasoned, not automatic from the PIL label.

examples.title: Region-specific public duty
examples.body: Residents of a district allege systemic failure of a state statutory welfare duty affecting a local class that cannot litigate individually. A bona fide petitioner moves the High Court under Article 226. The issue is whether Article 226 is the fit forum because of territory, other legal rights, and regional scale.

examples.title: Wrong territory
examples.body: A petition is filed in a High Court with no territorial link to the authority or the cause of action. The issue is whether liberalised standing can cure the want of territorial competence under Article 226.

examples.title: Private service dispute as 226 PIL
examples.body: An employee challenges a transfer as a 'PIL' in the High Court without a genuine public class injury. The issue is the private-dispute filter and possible costs under the limits topic.

hypotheticals.question: Can every public grievance be filed as Article 226 PIL in any High Court?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. The claim must engage a fundamental or other legal right, satisfy territorial competence, and meet bona fide public-interest standing. Forum shopping and private disputes fail.

hypotheticals.question: When is Article 226 preferable to Article 32 for a PIL?
hypotheticals.analysis: Often when the wrong is regional, involves other legal rights beyond Part III, or the High Court is the appropriate first forum. Article 32 remains the Supreme Court Part III gateway.

distinctions.left: Article 226: High Courts; fundamental rights and other legal rights; territorial limits.
distinctions.right: Article 32: Supreme Court; enforcement of fundamental rights.

rows.right: Petition may fail for want of standing or bona fides.

misconceptions.trap: Article 226 PIL has no territorial limits because standing is liberalised.
misconceptions.correction: Liberal standing does not remove territorial competence of the High Court.

misconceptions.trap: Article 226 and Article 32 are the same for every PIL.
misconceptions.correction: They differ in court, rights enforceable, and territorial structure; choose with reasons.

misconceptions.trap: Any statutory complaint becomes maintainable PIL in the High Court.
misconceptions.correction: The claim must still show a legal right or public duty, bona fides, and fitness for writ process; private disputes fail.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should an Article 226 PIL problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the fundamental or other legal right. II. Confirm territorial competence of the High Court. III. Test liberalised standing and bona fides. IV. Compare with Article 32 if forum is contested. V. Apply abuse filters. VI. State precise relief under Article 226.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Explain Public Interest Litigation under Article 226 of the Constitution.
questionsAndAnswers.answer: State Article 226 as the High Court gateway. Note the wider rights base (fundamental and other legal rights). Explain territorial limits. Describe liberalised standing within those limits. Contrast briefly with Article 32. Note abuse filters. Conclude that PIL is standing plus Article 226, not a new writ.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Discuss PIL under Article 226. Compare with Article 32 and examine territorial limits, standing, and abuse controls.
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Article 226 power and rights base. II. PIL as standing rule within Article 226. III. Territorial competence. IV. Liberal standing and bona fides. V. Comparison with Article 32 and forum choice. VI. Abuse filters and costs. VII. Worked forum/territory analysis. VIII. Conclusion: wide High Court access with territorial and bona fides limits.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should written submissions in an Article 226 PIL contain on forum and territory?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Identify the legal right; plead territorial facts linking the High Court; demonstrate bona fide public interest; answer any preference for Article 32 or another forum; and separate standing from the merits prayer while meeting abuse-filter objections.
